newsitem.title: MEXICO: INTERVIEW - Mexico PAN attacks PRI-PRD "collusion".
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Mexico PAN attacks PRI-PRD "collusion".

text.p: The conservative candidate for one of Mexico's top political jobs denounced "collusion" between the ruling Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI) and the other main opposition party to marginalise his party.

Carlos Castillo Peraza, the National Action Party (PAN) hopeful for mayor of Mexico City, saw his party take a commanding lead in early opinion polls to win the July 6 race but slump into second place after his candidacy was announced on March 2.

In an interview with Reuters, Castillo Peraza said he and his party were suffering vicious attacks because they were the only true alternative to the PRI system which has dominated Mexico since the 1910-17 Revolution.

Veteran left-wing Cuauhtemoc Cardenas and his Party of the Democratic Revolution (PRD) currently hold a big poll lead in the Mexico City race but Castillo Peraza noted that Cardenas spent most of his political career in the PRI, for whom he served as a state governor from 1980-86.
Other leading PRD figures, including its national leader Andres Manuel Lopez Obrador and its former chief Porfirio Munoz Ledo, have also come from the PRI.
Castillo said the PRD and the PRI "have joined forces to stop the PAN, which is the only different party, which has not come from the same history, the same PRI-ista culture."

PRD and PRI officials have agreed to organize a major television debate between their candidates on May 25 from which Castillo will be excluded, apparently because Cardenas is angered at the attacks Castillo has made on him.
"This debate shows the PRI-PRD collusion as members of a political family that has had country in its hands for so long," Castillo said in the interview, conducted last Friday night.

"For me, it's simple. If the PAN wins Mexico City and some local elections, the PAN will be ruling more than half of Mexico. That means the defeat of the PRI/PRD group which has controlled the country since 1915 or 1916."
"It's the group which has had the power, which has done the business, which has done the electoral frauds, they have controlled everything in the country."
"Separately they could lose...but now the PRI family has united against the PAN".
Castillo questioned Cardenas's record as a public official, saying official documents presented by the PAN showed Cardenas acted improperly in a land deal while governor of the state of Michoacan.

"Public documents show that as governor of Michoacan, Cardenas sold public land to his own mother at a ridiculous price," the PAN candidate said. "We believe that this shows a conduct which is not fit for him to aspire to govern again."

Cardenas has not denied that he transferred the beach property to his mother for a token sum. But he said the property previously belonged to an aunt who wanted to give it to his mother and left it temporarily in the hands of the state because of problems in sorting out the deeds.

Castillo said the PRD "had enjoyed a great silence of complicity on the part of the PRI" on this and other matters. "There has been a very open support (for Cardenas) by certain media who normally support the PRI," he added. "This makes us think that there is some deal done."

Opponents have also constantly hinted that Castillo Peraza is a homosexual and a religious extremist. The influential and generally pro-government Televisa television network has reported on more than one occasion rumours that Castillo dressed up as a butterfly, charges which angered him.

Asked about the allegations, Castillo said the PAN had suffered "months of attacks of every kind, on our private lives, against everything we do, every insignificant detail is being converted into something out of the ordinary, that is what we are fighting against."

In the din of the attacks, Castillo campaign officials have had trouble putting across their candidate's message for cleaning up the city's corrupt police force and stimulating tourism and health services to create jobs.

The PAN has also suffered in the polls. Respected local pollsters Indemerc/Louis Harris, who have tracked the Mexico City race since early last year, found that support for the PAN crashed to just 17.2 percent in May, its lowest yet.
Not only was Cardenas -- with 33 percent -- well clear of his rivals but the PAN risked losing second place to the PRI if current trends continued, Indemerc said.
